full_text:
Interviewer:	Ok I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing, to begin with so it’ll make sense to you.  We’re interviewing 2nd year women engineering students from all disciplines.  Are you going on placement?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	We’re mainly interviewing people that are going on placement because we want to know about what they’re expecting to get out of the placement and we’re hoping to go back to students, when they’re actually on the placement and interview them again (OK) to see what’s happening.  But we’re also going to be asking you about why you decided to do engineering and about your experiences of higher education so far (OK).  There is currently a lot of information out there saying that more women are going into engineering, but that they tend to leave, after a while, so we’re trying to see if anything happens in women’s first experiences of the industry that makes women decide that it’s not quite what they expected.  So at the end of the 2 year project, we’re going to put together a document to give to the Engineering Councils, and hopefully improve the situation for women in the industry. (OK)  So that’s the background to the project so I’m going to start by asking you some background questions about why you decided to go into engineering.  So is it chemical engineering that you’re doing?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	Biology, chemistry, maths and further maths, well further maths as an ‘AS’.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Went to a Grammar School.

Interviewer:	Was it a girls school?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	No, that’s Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	Yeah, my dad is a health & safety engineer, so he kind of – he didn’t do any – he did an apprenticeship (yeah) and then he just kind of worked his way up, and now he’s like

Interviewer:	 (phone rings and conversation takes place) Sorry about that.  Where was I? 

Subject:	With my dad. Yes, and now he’s a health & safety engineer, working in [town].

Interviewer:	Oh I’m from [town].

Subject:	Are you?

Interviewer:	Yes. Who does he work for?

Subject:	Well it used to be – they’ve been all sorts of things – [company].

Interviewer:	Yeah, everybody who lives in [town], knows at least one person who works there.  It’s one of the main employers. When and why do you think that you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	I don’t really know. I knew it would be a challenge and I had to do something that would be a challenge for me.  Erm, so I suppose it just st – well, the way you think about things like you think, is the way I do, erm but apart from that I really don’t know.  I just thought – I just woke – I don’t know – I was – when I went on courses on things er I – actually, well I was going to come to [this university] anyway, and I don’t know why I chose chemical engineering – it goes with my ‘A’ levels so.

Interviewer:	When you chose your ‘A’ levels did you have in mind anything that you wanted to do in future – why did you choose them ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	Erm, cos I – cos I enjoyed them. I was reasonably good at them – that’s the only reason I choose them. I was going to do sports science at ‘A’ level – sports studies sorry but I didn’t – because I’ve got hockey, I didn’t need to have done sports science to go on a sports science degree, so. That’s why I chose it.

Interviewer:	So when you was looking at courses, did you ever consider doing a maths at university, or something more – that was just one subject, at ‘A’ level or did you want something that would combine those ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	Yes combined definitely. I actually applied to do class and sports science here, and then chemistry and sports science as well, but I had to do – I couldn’t just do one thing, it had to be with something, either a dual honours or engineering.

Interviewer:	And why did you want to come to [this university] then, was that because of the sports?

Subject:	Because of the hockey here.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think the fact that your dad did engineering influenced you at all?

Subject:	Er, maybe a little bit.  Er, ‘cos I always talked to him about – cos I didn’t have a clue what I was going to do when I left school, and I had all these ideas and he would just be like now, what you going to do at the end of this?  And what actually are you going to achieve by doing this sort of degree?  You know, this, that and the other.  Erm, so in that respect, like just talking to him and a few other people as well, erm I was looking for something that would be reasonably worthwhile, because there’s no way that – like I don’t think sports science was the one because everyone does sports science.  So.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what do you think it is, about engineering that makes it worthwhile then?

Subject:	Erm, because they’re short of engineers – female engineers, so you’re more employable.  There aren’t that many out there really so.

Interviewer:	OK, did you have any careers advice when you were at school?

Subject:	Mm, yeah, it was shocking – no, it was shocking.  I can’t remember – I was told all sorts of rubbish and but I didn’t really pay any attention to it.

Interviewer:	OK, What appeals to you about doing chemical engineering?  Did you ever consider doing any of the other engineering disciplines?

Subject:	Not really.  Erm, ‘cos like chemistry’s ace and I couldn’t see myself – I’m not really – I’m not really interested in cars or planes or anything to do like them things and civil engineering – not – I don’t think so – so erm, so no I didn’t really look at any others.  I looked at chemical engineering and that’s all – that’s all I applied to do or you know, the other 2 courses here.  So – I don’t know why.

Interviewer:	What do you think is good about chemical engineering specifically then?  You said a bit about the way you have to think and things like that?

Subject:	Er, what’s good about it?  God, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. When you applied to the course, did you know you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK I’ll come back, to talk about that later then.  When you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah.  I knew it would be.

Interviewer:	Did that ever bother you at all?

Subject:	No.  Not at all.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely but I mean I can see why women don’t.

Interviewer:	Why?

Subject:	Well it’s just – er, the blokes, to be honest, are an absolute nightmare.  Like a lot – well a lot are gradually getting better and stuff but now, I’ve nearly finished my second year and some of them still completely discard any opinion you have, because you’re a female.  And it’s like come on, (look at the year we’re in?), it shouldn’t be like that at all but you just have to deal with it. If you’ve got the confidence to do it then you’ll be absolutely fine, but I can see why a lot of women don’t because it is really chauvinistic to be fair.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that women know enough about what engineering is to make a decision whether to study it or not?

Subject:	Probably not – probably not.  Er I think the only reason that women – I don’t think – no-one really on my course – females on my course, had previous experience. They just, they’ve kind of just done it and a lot of blokes have and like they did years out in engineering type things. And I don’t think that opportunity is really there for women at all.

Interviewer:	What do you think would need to be done, in sort of an early stage, to encourage more – or give women the opportunity to get into engineering then?

Subject:	The chance to do work experience.  I mean when you’re in –I did a week, 2 weeks experience – that was in my GCSE year and stuff, but don’t really like – like in my area people like want to just be like nursing, or looking after kids that kind of thing and it is like that – or teaching.  Erm, but I mean that’s just from where they’re – cos where I live, I live near [town] so there is a lot of chemical engineering going on around there but actually where I live it’s – you know people just tend to do GCSE’s and that’s it.  So – but I think, I think, yeah, just to be given an opportunity like to be looked on as equal, when you’re in – you know when you’re in year 10 or 11, to be looked as equal to a male, to do that job. Also, just give them a chance, so there.
Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics then, do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Make a good engineer?  You have to think on your feet.  And what generally – like doing my course or actually being an engineer?

Interviewer:	Well, I suppose from your experience it’ll be doing your course but so yeah.

Subject:	Erm, you’ve got to store a lot at the moment. I mean hopefully when I graduate it’ll all be in books, so it’ll be alright and it’ll be different thinking then. But erm, just a – you know, to be able to think on your feet and go with it.  To have the confidence to go with it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that those are traditionally thought of as more male characteristics.?

Subject:	Yeah – definitely, yeah. But its changing, isn’t it?

Interviewer:	Yeah. OK, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	What on my course or in the future?

Interviewer:	Both?

Subject:	Ok, the advantages – I think I’m more employable because it’s just different. I suppose most companies are all male engineers – I mean I’ve actually looked around a few and stuff, for my placement yeah, and they are – it is very male dominated, and I think to have a female on like the team, would add a different perspective and a different way of looking at and thinking about problems and things.  So I think I’m more employable.  On my course, advantages – I’m not afraid to ask for help. If it – it doesn’t bother me going to sort out problems, because a lot of blokes it does because we have to do group work and they won’t – they just won’t.  The disadvantages – just male opinions, like the way they look at all kind of – it’s not the same kind of respect, if you see what I mean.  ‘cos they’ve got their male friends and they have their female friends when it comes to like doing problems and things.

Interviewer:	Yeah, why do you think that is?

Subject:	I don’t know.

Interviewer:	How do you deal with that when they are…then?

Subject:	I ignore it now I think.  I completely ignore it.

Interviewer:	Have you found that’s the best way?

Subject:	Well, there’s only – now there’s only like a few guys that are like that and I don’t know – what’s the point?  It’s a waste of space, isn’t it?  I think – I just think there’s no point bothering (yeah). I just – they’re not prepared to like the change the way – the way they think or look at you, or whatever, so there’s just no – I can’t be bothered to waste my time with them, so.

Interviewer:	OK, how many girls are there, on your course?

Subject:	Quite a lot actually.

Interviewer:	More than you expected there to be?

Subject:	Yeah, a lot more than I expected.  Erm, cos a lot from overseas as well.  Erm, I suppose there’s a good third.

Interviewer:	Really?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	That’s quite high. Has the course been what you expected it to be in other respects?

Subject:	I didn’t really have any like you know, thoughts of what it would be like, at all really.  Just a – there’s a lot more on physics than I thought there would be.  So apart from that, I didn’t really have any …

Interviewer:	What then do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, best thing is being – doing the design, because this year we do 4 different design projects and we work in teams. Erm, and that’s brilliant, ‘cos that’s what I’m gonna do next year as well.  And that’s just been brilliant – it’s like giving us a huge problem – a real like problem, to solve and it’s – well try and solve, and it’s really good, I like that.

Interviewer:	Is it the actual work that you like doing or working as a team, or both?

Subject:	Er, both really. I mean like – the last one we did, like working in a team was absolutely brilliant and then we had to – well, I was working with another guy and we had to like design a whole plant.  And that was brilliant, because I love doing that.  And then, we got to take it back to the group to show them and just – it was really good, the whole thing. It’s like working as a team to achieve something, and it actually pays off and I just think that’s really cool.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of doing group work?

Subject:	Erm, the advantage is you’ve got more – more ideas, more thoughts, so you get a – you should come up with the best solution or er you know, (??) or something.  Disadvantages – you get sort of people that really don’t – aren’t bothered.  Like at the moment, in my group, all of them are just sort of like, whatever.  And it’s – you know.  You get it, ‘cos it does slow you down a lot when you get that…

Interviewer:	Have you been put into that group?

Subject:	Yeah, all the groups are just – someone, someone does – I don’t know. Erm, yeah, because the groups are quite small – they’re only sort of 5 or 6.  If you get 3 people that really don’t – aren’t bothered – you can’t – the rest of you can’t do the work, so that’s the disadvantage, just people not caring.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer to work with men or women, or aren’t you bothered?

Subject:	It doesn’t bother me.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Like what?

Subject:	Erm, the blokes – a lot of the time, the blokes will just go off and do the work and they just won’t look at what they’re doing.  So they’ll just keep going, going, going and they get this number at the end and it’ll be completely – you know – just rubbish, just – it wouldn’t work or whatever, but then they think it’s fine because they’ve done it.  Whereas women are more like, you know, they’ll do it, make sure it’s right and – and I think that women are a lot more organised as well. Like it comes to like – because we have regular group meetings, the women are all there, on time, with their work. That’s it really.

Interviewer:	That makes it sound like women are better at doing group work than men, so do you still think you don’t mind whether you work with men or women?

Subject:	No, I don’t mind because – the way blokes do things as well – you know women – I don’t know…

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s best to have a combination then rather than just be all men or all women?

Subject:	Definitely, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the group work that you’ve done will help you when you go to work in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely, definitely, because I’m working in a team next year, so – I think it’s all – all blokes next year maybe – I don’t know.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think have been the worst things about the course?

Subject:	Fluid mechanics.  Erm, just – yeah, a couple of modules have been awful.  They’ve just been so hard it’s really hard.

Interviewer:	Is that to do with teaching or just the subject generally do you think?

Subject:	Occasionally it’s to do with the teaching.  Erm, and – the notes that you get are just like rubbish.  But er, no, no, just a couple of modules have been just hard and horrible, but I think, apart from that – I mean obviously the work load is quite big and we have a lot of hours and things but it’s fine.  But I just think a couple of the modules are a bit horrible.

Interviewer:	OK, you obviously put in a lot more hours, within the university, than students in say social sciences, or humanities or something – do you think that will prepare you more for when you get into the industry?

Subject:	I don’t know. I think – I mean, yeah, it should do I should think, because you have to kind of go to lectures and things and I don’t know, I think that anyone – it doesn’t matter what they do, when they get that job they’ll want to do that job and they’ll be prepared to get up at work time and work for however long they need to, so I don’t – I think, at the end of the day, if you – you know, work for a degree and get the job that you want, you will do whatever.  So I don’t think it really matters.

Interviewer:	OK, are you pleased you chose this course?

Subject:	Ask me that in another year.  Yeah, 

Interviewer:	Have you enjoyed it, on the whole, so far?

Subject:	Er, yeah, I suppose. I don’t – sometimes I’m just like, you know, I mean next year will definitely make or break whether I do an MEng, or a BEng and what I do in the future. But a lot of people have said to me, after their year out, they’ve just become more – like a lot better at the course. It’s like the way they are, they’ve just become more confident and things, so hopefully I’ll be one of them and it’ll be alright.

Interviewer:	OK. We’ll come back and talk about the placement, a bit more later. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	None?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	Would you have liked to have been taught by some female lecturers?

Subject:	It would have been nice, but it doesn’t really matter, I don’t think.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be encouraging at all?

Subject:	Hmm

Interviewer:	Thinking like if they can do it, I can do it sort of thing?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it’d be – like for the freshers and for when people come on visits and things before they’re even at uni.  It would be quite nice to see some females in the department, because I came to the department a couple of times before and the only females that were in there, work in reception – secretaries, you know, and that doesn’t inspire any sign of confidence at all (yeah).  But – it would be nice but there we go.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

Subject:	Yes and no.

Interviewer:	What some of them do and some of them don’t?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah definitely some of them do, some of them don’t.

Interviewer:	The ones that don’t – how do they treat you differently?

Subject:	It’s not so bad any more because they know us.  But initially they were just like – I don’t know there was just something different. I can’t put my finger on it but they just – you can tell but it’s …

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that’s because they’re not used to teaching women yet?

Subject:	Yeah, there is quite a lot of women on my course and I suppose there’s a lot more than there is in other years as well, so I suppose that might have something to do with it, but they should be used to it.  I don’t know it’s a bit weird that one.

Interviewer:	Do you feel with the male students and teachers then that because you’re a woman you have to work twice as hard to prove that you can do it?

Subject:	Yeah, I used to a bit but it’s only with certain people. I mean their views are changing all the time, it just depends who you’re with really.  The kind of group you’re in, or you know, who’s around but usually not.

Interviewer:	Is your personal tutor male as well then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are you happy that you’ve got that personal tutor, are they approachable?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely - definitely

Interviewer:	Yeah, you wouldn’t rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	No, because with my personal tutor, he used to play hockey, so he understands hockey as well, which is why he’s so spot on.  Which is probably I’ve got that tutor.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?  

Subject:	Erm, not really.  I don’t know – there’s a couple of – well a couple on my course keep me going really.

Interviewer:	Yeah, like they motivate you.

Subject:	Yeah, it’s just like tell me to actually do some work and you know not just keep training and playing and socialising…

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think there any bits of the teaching or advice that will particularly help you on your placement?

Subject:	I don’t – I don’t know what to expect really, I mean I’ve been round, I’ve been to the company like twice and met them all and stuff and but I…

Interviewer:	Who is it that you’re going to?

Subject:	 [Company], its in [town].  And like when I go there I will do – well 2 or 3 weeks overlap with the person that’s already there, so she’ll like help me with that and (save up?) projects and things. I don’t know what I need to know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will use like the technical skills and the knowledge that you’ve learnt on the course.  Do you think you will actually put that into use?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely because I’ll be kind of erm problem solving.  And I mean obviously, all the information’s in the book but if you don’t know how to use it, then you can’t do anything, so yeah, I should think I will be all the time.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll be using a lot of your generic skills, like team working and things like that as well?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, Do you feel like you’re ready and prepared to go on placement now?

Subject:	Just about.  Just about.  Erm, I’m sure it’ll be absolutely fine, just be yourself and it’ll be alright.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university could do anything else to prepare you for what it’s going to be like in industry?

Subject:	No, I mean we do – like I said we do lots of team work and things and I don’t really know what else we’re gonna – I don’t know what to expect but I don’t think the university can do that. I think it should be up to you to go to the company and sort things out for yourself.

Interviewer:	Have you spoken to many people that have been on the placement before?

Subject:	Yeah, only cos I know a lot of finalists and things now so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that helps you at all?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, I mean they’re just – they just say how good it is, and it doesn’t put you off at all when everyone’s like, yeah, it was brilliant, best year, and 

Interviewer:	No-one’s had any bad experiences then?

Subject:	No, because anyone who had a bad experience, isn’t doing the degree any more so.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you want to go on the placement then?

Subject:	To get some experience (yeah) because I haven’t got any.  And again I’ll be more employable I think, as well.  Yeah, just to really get some experience and see what’s going on – I mean I could have done – I don’t know – just sort of put everything into practice. I like doing things practically and goes in more.

Interviewer:	OK, what attracted you to the company that you’re going to work for?

Subject:	Ha ha, how shallow am I going to sound right now?  Erm, well I got offered a job there and I got offered a – a choice of 3 places, at another company and they were companies down in London, so I played them off against each other a bit.  Er, I got a salary increase and the company I’m going to now is near home, it’s almost what I want to do because they basically let me choose, and I’m sponsored and it’s a pretty reasonable salary as well, so.

Interviewer:	So was pay quite an important factor for you then when you were looking at different companies?

Subject:	It wasn’t because like when you – you put your name down for different things, and you don’t know what the salary is.

Interviewer:	Just the situation let you?

Subject:	Yeah if it had just been – if I had just got one job, I would’ve just taken it, kind of thing, cos I only really wanted things I would be interested in, and I only wanted – I only went for the one in [town] because it’s near home and, but at the end of the day if you can do that then it’s – becomes more of a factor, than it would do normally.

Interviewer:	When you were looking at companies, did you look at things like training opportunities, and career prospects for when you’ve finished your degree and things like that?

Subject:	Not really, I just looked at the types of industry that I wanted to go into.  I just put my name down for them really.

Interviewer:	OK, and did you say it’s the design side that you want to go into more?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you do much research into the different companies then?

Subject:	Erm, yeah I researched them a bit when I put my name down and then when I went to interview obviously I read up on them and stuff – but I only really had – I got a job pretty quickly so I didn’t have many interviews, so I didn’t research that many.

Interviewer:	Do you know what type of work you’ll be doing when you get there?  Have they told you much about what to expect?

Subject:	Yeah, I’ll be doing – I’ll probably end – I’ll have several projects on the go all the time.  Part of them long term, some short term and erm, just general – well, like they’ll have certain problems like they want to save so much money on this, or they want to get this out but – and I’ll just – it’s up to me to do it, and research it and sort it out, kind of thing.  I mean – obviously it’s not going to be huge and major but I mean like one project that I’m going to get which is – the girl that’s there at the moment, she’s going to – and they’ll try and – they have kind of 8 machines, for sort of – they all do the same thing, and they want to use 6 but increase the output, so that’s one big thing.

Interviewer:	OK, what are you most looking forward to about going on placement?

Subject:	Working with real people.  Big people – because it is a bit of a bubble, and you don’t see many people, and that’ll be nice to like actually go out and just like learn stuff properly, rather than just be sat in a lecture theatre – actually really learn stuff.

Interviewer:	OK and is there anything that you’re apprehensive or concerned about?

Subject:	No, no, I’ve heard well, as long as I’m confident in myself, then I’ll be alright.

Interviewer:	OK, how involved were the university in helping you find a placement?

Subject:	They were really good erm they kind of – obviously the companies approach the department and say we want to interview on  this day.  But there’s a board on – next to the notice board, with lists up, like name of company, where it is and you just write your name down on there. And then all your – the department sends all your CV’s – CV’s that are on the list, to the company who kind of choose some people they want to interview.  So they’re brilliant like that because a lot of people actually have to go out and send out their own CV and do all that, but our department were brilliant, absolutely brilliant.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there is anything else that they should be doing or shouldn’t be doing, to help you?

Subject:	No, I mean they’ve got – they’ve also got all the research and things because all these companies obviously send out their things and you can look at all that. I don’t think so – I mean they’ve obviously been doing that kind of thing for years because they’ve got it down to a fine art now.  So no, I don’t think they can do anymore.

Interviewer:	OK, your department’s obviously one of the better ones.  You mentioned about getting sponsorship. (yeah). Are you sponsored at the minute or is that…

Subject:	Yeah, well the company that I’m going to, offered me sponsorship so – and that’s just while I’m doing my degree.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of having sponsorship?

Subject:	The only advantage is money.  There’s no disadvantages because I don’t have to work for them when I graduate. So it’s a really weird one. I can’t understand that but that’s fine.

Interviewer:	They must hope that you will work for them, or something?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean it – cos in the contract it just kind of says I’m not obliged to work there but if there’s an opening, then chances are I’ll get the job over someone else. So it’s a weird one.

Interviewer:	If you get on OK on your placement would you be happy to go and work for them when you’ve finished?

Subject:	Different location, but yeah.  Because their company’s – they work well.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, what do you see yourself doing then in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Oh God.  Let’s have a think.  I’ll probably have been working for 2 years.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you will be in the chemical engineering industry?

Subject:	I should think so. I should think so.  I’ll know in a few months – if I don’t I might do a second degree, but I don’t know – yeah, if I’m working it’ll probably be that.

Interviewer:	What about more long term, do you think that you’d like to go down the managerial route or become more specialist?

Subject:	Become specialised.  Well no – long term, I’d like to retire young.  And then like, do something like coaching and stuff – that’d be fun.  But, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	OK, what then would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Ideal career?  Oh, design engineer would be quite nice – an amazing hockey coach – I don’t know.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in chemical engineering?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Is that in terms of getting into the industry and once you’re in the industry for moving upwards?

Subject:	Yeah, cos I mean usually like – from what I’ve seen – and a company will have sort of 3 or 4 mechanical engineers and 1 chemical engineer.  So if you’re like the chemical engineer then obviously you’re a lot – you know, there’s 4 of them, there’s only 1 of you, they’re not going to get rid of you unless – well, it’s pretty highly unlikely that they’re gonna get rid of you, when they have job cuts and things as well, so in that respect…

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you have done anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d probably have done slightly different ‘A’ levels.

Interviewer:	Why? If you’d done different ‘A’ levels, do you still think you’d be where you are now?

Subject:	I’d be at [this university]. Sometimes I wonder why I did chemical engineering.  Erm, I probably would have done like sports science and chemistry. I don’t know – it is a lot of work.  I’m like, I’d like to not do as much.

Interviewer:	But it’s interesting to hear you say that. Because you think you probably will go into the chemical engineering industry, but there probably are other things that you could do.

Subject:	Yeah. Ideally I’d work for sort of 9 months in a proper job and for 3 months I’d – I’d love to do something outside but it’s just like you don’t really have to think about it – it’s easy – easy on the brain, that would be quite good, because I love being outside, doing adventure schemes, but only like a very few people can do that.  And I know a couple of people that do, which is probably why I’m like, so envious of them.

Interviewer:	But do you think that’s not a realistic option to you then?

Subject:	Not really.  The chances are slim.  If the opportunity came up then I’d do it.  But I’m not – I wouldn’t – it wouldn’t bother me if I don’t ever do it, kind of thing, so.

Interviewer:	OK. What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the chemical engineering industry or your experience of it so far?

Subject:	That’s a tough one.  Erm, (long pause) it depends what you look at though.  Like it depends which kind of bit of the industry you look at.  Erm, diverse, (long pause).

Interviewer:	Would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	Yeah.
.
Interviewer:	Do you think that it is masculine just because of the numbers of males in the industry or do you think it’s more than that?

Subject:	Generally, the numbers of males in the industry.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it’ll stay like that or do you think that there will be more women coming into the industry?

Subject:	I think gradually, there will be more women in the industry but it’ll always be male dominated – always.  Certainly for – well, while I’m alive I should think, to be honest.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is?

Subject:	Because that’s the way it’s always been – very traditional people aren’t we?

Interviewer:	Yes. But it’s changed in other industries, like in medicine and law and things like that.

Subject:	Yeah, it’s just – I don’t know, I just think it always will be in our lives.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s about the type of work you are doing as well?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	That it’s perceived as masculine work?

Subject:	Yeah, cos I mean you could – you could work on like – well, people work on an oil rig, and there’s chemical engineers on there and there’s no women on there (yeah) so – and then like if you look at the forces as well.  You get a – if you get a couple of – well, any engineers in there, in the forces – well, it is male dominated anyway there, isn’t it? (yeah) And then petro-chemicals again – ‘cos I wouldn’t work in – cos a lot – well no one on my course really wants to go in petro-chemicals but a couple are, but that’s just because I suppose how you see it and how you think about things.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that women that have done chemical engineering degrees, take it a different route to males then?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d say women tend to go into pharmaceuticals and food more, and men kind of more petro-chemical that kind of thing, more blokey stuff.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the fact that it is so masculine will cause you any problems or…?

Subject:	No.  No.

Interviewer:	Why not? Do you think that’s because you’ve made a decision to sort of stick to the design side or..?

Subject:	I think whatever area I work in, if it was full of men, it wouldn’t bother me at all but that’s probably just because of my personality and just probably because I play sport as well. It’s just something about my character I suppose, I don’t know.  But it just doesn’t bother me – it really doesn’t bother me.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it might bother men that you’re working with though?  That you’re a woman in their environment?

Subject:	Probably. They can deal with it.  Yeah, probably – maybe a little bit, gradually less and less I think.  But yeah, probably – a tiny bit.

Interviewer:	But that doesn’t bother you?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK that’s everything thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing, to begin with so it’ll make sense to you. We’re interviewing 2nd year women engineering students from all disciplines. Are you going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: We’re mainly interviewing people that are going on placement because we want to know about what they’re expecting to get out of the placement and we’re hoping to go back to students, when they’re actually on the placement and interview them again (OK) to see what’s happening. But we’re also going to be asking you about why you decided to do engineering and about your experiences of higher education so far (OK). There is currently a lot of information out there saying that more women are going into engineering, but that they tend to leave, after a while, so we’re trying to see if anything happens in women’s first experiences of the industry that makes women decide that it’s not quite what they expected. So at the end of the 2 year project, we’re going to put together a document to give to the Engineering Councils, and hopefully improve the situation for women in the industry. (OK) So that’s the background to the project so I’m going to start by asking you some background questions about why you decided to go into engineering. So is it chemical engineering that you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What ‘A’ levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Biology, chemistry, maths and further maths, well further maths as an ‘AS’.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Went to a Grammar School.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it a girls school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, that’s Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are either of your parents engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, my dad is a health & safety engineer, so he kind of – he didn’t do any – he did an apprenticeship (yeah) and then he just kind of worked his way up, and now he’s like

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: (phone rings and conversation takes place) Sorry about that. Where was I?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: With my dad. Yes, and now he’s a health & safety engineer, working in [town].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh I’m from [town].

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Are you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. Who does he work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it used to be – they’ve been all sorts of things – [company].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, everybody who lives in [town], knows at least one person who works there. It’s one of the main employers. When and why do you think that you decided to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really know. I knew it would be a challenge and I had to do something that would be a challenge for me. Erm, so I suppose it just st – well, the way you think about things like you think, is the way I do, erm but apart from that I really don’t know. I just thought – I just woke – I don’t know – I was – when I went on courses on things er I – actually, well I was going to come to [this university] anyway, and I don’t know why I chose chemical engineering – it goes with my ‘A’ levels so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you chose your ‘A’ levels did you have in mind anything that you wanted to do in future – why did you choose them ‘A’ levels?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, cos I – cos I enjoyed them. I was reasonably good at them – that’s the only reason I choose them. I was going to do sports science at ‘A’ level – sports studies sorry but I didn’t – because I’ve got hockey, I didn’t need to have done sports science to go on a sports science degree, so. That’s why I chose it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So when you was looking at courses, did you ever consider doing a maths at university, or something more – that was just one subject, at ‘A’ level or did you want something that would combine those ‘A’ levels?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes combined definitely. I actually applied to do class and sports science here, and then chemistry and sports science as well, but I had to do – I couldn’t just do one thing, it had to be with something, either a dual honours or engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And why did you want to come to [this university] then, was that because of the sports?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because of the hockey here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think the fact that your dad did engineering influenced you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, maybe a little bit. Er, ‘cos I always talked to him about – cos I didn’t have a clue what I was going to do when I left school, and I had all these ideas and he would just be like now, what you going to do at the end of this? And what actually are you going to achieve by doing this sort of degree? You know, this, that and the other. Erm, so in that respect, like just talking to him and a few other people as well, erm I was looking for something that would be reasonably worthwhile, because there’s no way that – like I don’t think sports science was the one because everyone does sports science. So.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what do you think it is, about engineering that makes it worthwhile then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, because they’re short of engineers – female engineers, so you’re more employable. There aren’t that many out there really so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you have any careers advice when you were at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, yeah, it was shocking – no, it was shocking. I can’t remember – I was told all sorts of rubbish and but I didn’t really pay any attention to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What appeals to you about doing chemical engineering? Did you ever consider doing any of the other engineering disciplines?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. Erm, ‘cos like chemistry’s ace and I couldn’t see myself – I’m not really – I’m not really interested in cars or planes or anything to do like them things and civil engineering – not – I don’t think so – so erm, so no I didn’t really look at any others. I looked at chemical engineering and that’s all – that’s all I applied to do or you know, the other 2 courses here. So – I don’t know why.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think is good about chemical engineering specifically then? You said a bit about the way you have to think and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, what’s good about it? God, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s OK. When you applied to the course, did you know you wanted to do a sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK I’ll come back, to talk about that later then. When you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I knew it would be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did that ever bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Not at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely but I mean I can see why women don’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it’s just – er, the blokes, to be honest, are an absolute nightmare. Like a lot – well a lot are gradually getting better and stuff but now, I’ve nearly finished my second year and some of them still completely discard any opinion you have, because you’re a female. And it’s like come on, (look at the year we’re in?), it shouldn’t be like that at all but you just have to deal with it. If you’ve got the confidence to do it then you’ll be absolutely fine, but I can see why a lot of women don’t because it is really chauvinistic to be fair.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that women know enough about what engineering is to make a decision whether to study it or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably not – probably not. Er I think the only reason that women – I don’t think – no-one really on my course – females on my course, had previous experience. They just, they’ve kind of just done it and a lot of blokes have and like they did years out in engineering type things. And I don’t think that opportunity is really there for women at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think would need to be done, in sort of an early stage, to encourage more – or give women the opportunity to get into engineering then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The chance to do work experience. I mean when you’re in –I did a week, 2 weeks experience – that was in my GCSE year and stuff, but don’t really like – like in my area people like want to just be like nursing, or looking after kids that kind of thing and it is like that – or teaching. Erm, but I mean that’s just from where they’re – cos where I live, I live near [town] so there is a lot of chemical engineering going on around there but actually where I live it’s – you know people just tend to do GCSE’s and that’s it. So – but I think, I think, yeah, just to be given an opportunity like to be looked on as equal, when you’re in – you know when you’re in year 10 or 11, to be looked as equal to a male, to do that job. Also, just give them a chance, so there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics then, do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Make a good engineer? You have to think on your feet. And what generally – like doing my course or actually being an engineer?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well, I suppose from your experience it’ll be doing your course but so yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, you’ve got to store a lot at the moment. I mean hopefully when I graduate it’ll all be in books, so it’ll be alright and it’ll be different thinking then. But erm, just a – you know, to be able to think on your feet and go with it. To have the confidence to go with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that those are traditionally thought of as more male characteristics.?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – definitely, yeah. But its changing, isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. OK, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What on my course or in the future?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Both?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ok, the advantages – I think I’m more employable because it’s just different. I suppose most companies are all male engineers – I mean I’ve actually looked around a few and stuff, for my placement yeah, and they are – it is very male dominated, and I think to have a female on like the team, would add a different perspective and a different way of looking at and thinking about problems and things. So I think I’m more employable. On my course, advantages – I’m not afraid to ask for help. If it – it doesn’t bother me going to sort out problems, because a lot of blokes it does because we have to do group work and they won’t – they just won’t. The disadvantages – just male opinions, like the way they look at all kind of – it’s not the same kind of respect, if you see what I mean. ‘cos they’ve got their male friends and they have their female friends when it comes to like doing problems and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, why do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you deal with that when they are…then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I ignore it now I think. I completely ignore it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you found that’s the best way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, there’s only – now there’s only like a few guys that are like that and I don’t know – what’s the point? It’s a waste of space, isn’t it? I think – I just think there’s no point bothering (yeah). I just – they’re not prepared to like the change the way – the way they think or look at you, or whatever, so there’s just no – I can’t be bothered to waste my time with them, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how many girls are there, on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Quite a lot actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: More than you expected there to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, a lot more than I expected. Erm, cos a lot from overseas as well. Erm, I suppose there’s a good third.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s quite high. Has the course been what you expected it to be in other respects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t really have any like you know, thoughts of what it would be like, at all really. Just a – there’s a lot more on physics than I thought there would be. So apart from that, I didn’t really have any …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What then do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, best thing is being – doing the design, because this year we do 4 different design projects and we work in teams. Erm, and that’s brilliant, ‘cos that’s what I’m gonna do next year as well. And that’s just been brilliant – it’s like giving us a huge problem – a real like problem, to solve and it’s – well try and solve, and it’s really good, I like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it the actual work that you like doing or working as a team, or both?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, both really. I mean like – the last one we did, like working in a team was absolutely brilliant and then we had to – well, I was working with another guy and we had to like design a whole plant. And that was brilliant, because I love doing that. And then, we got to take it back to the group to show them and just – it was really good, the whole thing. It’s like working as a team to achieve something, and it actually pays off and I just think that’s really cool.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the advantage is you’ve got more – more ideas, more thoughts, so you get a – you should come up with the best solution or er you know, (??) or something. Disadvantages – you get sort of people that really don’t – aren’t bothered. Like at the moment, in my group, all of them are just sort of like, whatever. And it’s – you know. You get it, ‘cos it does slow you down a lot when you get that…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been put into that group?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, all the groups are just – someone, someone does – I don’t know. Erm, yeah, because the groups are quite small – they’re only sort of 5 or 6. If you get 3 people that really don’t – aren’t bothered – you can’t – the rest of you can’t do the work, so that’s the disadvantage, just people not caring.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer to work with men or women, or aren’t you bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn’t bother me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like what?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the blokes – a lot of the time, the blokes will just go off and do the work and they just won’t look at what they’re doing. So they’ll just keep going, going, going and they get this number at the end and it’ll be completely – you know – just rubbish, just – it wouldn’t work or whatever, but then they think it’s fine because they’ve done it. Whereas women are more like, you know, they’ll do it, make sure it’s right and – and I think that women are a lot more organised as well. Like it comes to like – because we have regular group meetings, the women are all there, on time, with their work. That’s it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That makes it sound like women are better at doing group work than men, so do you still think you don’t mind whether you work with men or women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t mind because – the way blokes do things as well – you know women – I don’t know…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s best to have a combination then rather than just be all men or all women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the group work that you’ve done will help you when you go to work in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely, definitely, because I’m working in a team next year, so – I think it’s all – all blokes next year maybe – I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think have been the worst things about the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Fluid mechanics. Erm, just – yeah, a couple of modules have been awful. They’ve just been so hard it’s really hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that to do with teaching or just the subject generally do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Occasionally it’s to do with the teaching. Erm, and – the notes that you get are just like rubbish. But er, no, no, just a couple of modules have been just hard and horrible, but I think, apart from that – I mean obviously the work load is quite big and we have a lot of hours and things but it’s fine. But I just think a couple of the modules are a bit horrible.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you obviously put in a lot more hours, within the university, than students in say social sciences, or humanities or something – do you think that will prepare you more for when you get into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I think – I mean, yeah, it should do I should think, because you have to kind of go to lectures and things and I don’t know, I think that anyone – it doesn’t matter what they do, when they get that job they’ll want to do that job and they’ll be prepared to get up at work time and work for however long they need to, so I don’t – I think, at the end of the day, if you – you know, work for a degree and get the job that you want, you will do whatever. So I don’t think it really matters.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you pleased you chose this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ask me that in another year. Yeah,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you enjoyed it, on the whole, so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah, I suppose. I don’t – sometimes I’m just like, you know, I mean next year will definitely make or break whether I do an MEng, or a BEng and what I do in the future. But a lot of people have said to me, after their year out, they’ve just become more – like a lot better at the course. It’s like the way they are, they’ve just become more confident and things, so hopefully I’ll be one of them and it’ll be alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. We’ll come back and talk about the placement, a bit more later. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: None?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you have liked to have been taught by some female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It would have been nice, but it doesn’t really matter, I don’t think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be encouraging at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Thinking like if they can do it, I can do it sort of thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it’d be – like for the freshers and for when people come on visits and things before they’re even at uni. It would be quite nice to see some females in the department, because I came to the department a couple of times before and the only females that were in there, work in reception – secretaries, you know, and that doesn’t inspire any sign of confidence at all (yeah). But – it would be nice but there we go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes and no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What some of them do and some of them don’t?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah definitely some of them do, some of them don’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The ones that don’t – how do they treat you differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s not so bad any more because they know us. But initially they were just like – I don’t know there was just something different. I can’t put my finger on it but they just – you can tell but it’s …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that’s because they’re not used to teaching women yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there is quite a lot of women on my course and I suppose there’s a lot more than there is in other years as well, so I suppose that might have something to do with it, but they should be used to it. I don’t know it’s a bit weird that one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel with the male students and teachers then that because you’re a woman you have to work twice as hard to prove that you can do it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I used to a bit but it’s only with certain people. I mean their views are changing all the time, it just depends who you’re with really. The kind of group you’re in, or you know, who’s around but usually not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is your personal tutor male as well then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy that you’ve got that personal tutor, are they approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely - definitely

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, you wouldn’t rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because with my personal tutor, he used to play hockey, so he understands hockey as well, which is why he’s so spot on. Which is probably I’ve got that tutor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. I don’t know – there’s a couple of – well a couple on my course keep me going really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, like they motivate you.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s just like tell me to actually do some work and you know not just keep training and playing and socialising…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think there any bits of the teaching or advice that will particularly help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t – I don’t know what to expect really, I mean I’ve been round, I’ve been to the company like twice and met them all and stuff and but I…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Who is it that you’re going to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Company], its in [town]. And like when I go there I will do – well 2 or 3 weeks overlap with the person that’s already there, so she’ll like help me with that and (save up?) projects and things. I don’t know what I need to know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will use like the technical skills and the knowledge that you’ve learnt on the course. Do you think you will actually put that into use?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely because I’ll be kind of erm problem solving. And I mean obviously, all the information’s in the book but if you don’t know how to use it, then you can’t do anything, so yeah, I should think I will be all the time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll be using a lot of your generic skills, like team working and things like that as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Do you feel like you’re ready and prepared to go on placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just about. Just about. Erm, I’m sure it’ll be absolutely fine, just be yourself and it’ll be alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university could do anything else to prepare you for what it’s going to be like in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I mean we do – like I said we do lots of team work and things and I don’t really know what else we’re gonna – I don’t know what to expect but I don’t think the university can do that. I think it should be up to you to go to the company and sort things out for yourself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you spoken to many people that have been on the placement before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, only cos I know a lot of finalists and things now so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that helps you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, I mean they’re just – they just say how good it is, and it doesn’t put you off at all when everyone’s like, yeah, it was brilliant, best year, and

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No-one’s had any bad experiences then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because anyone who had a bad experience, isn’t doing the degree any more so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you want to go on the placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To get some experience (yeah) because I haven’t got any. And again I’ll be more employable I think, as well. Yeah, just to really get some experience and see what’s going on – I mean I could have done – I don’t know – just sort of put everything into practice. I like doing things practically and goes in more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what attracted you to the company that you’re going to work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ha ha, how shallow am I going to sound right now? Erm, well I got offered a job there and I got offered a – a choice of 3 places, at another company and they were companies down in London, so I played them off against each other a bit. Er, I got a salary increase and the company I’m going to now is near home, it’s almost what I want to do because they basically let me choose, and I’m sponsored and it’s a pretty reasonable salary as well, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So was pay quite an important factor for you then when you were looking at different companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It wasn’t because like when you – you put your name down for different things, and you don’t know what the salary is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Just the situation let you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah if it had just been – if I had just got one job, I would’ve just taken it, kind of thing, cos I only really wanted things I would be interested in, and I only wanted – I only went for the one in [town] because it’s near home and, but at the end of the day if you can do that then it’s – becomes more of a factor, than it would do normally.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you were looking at companies, did you look at things like training opportunities, and career prospects for when you’ve finished your degree and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, I just looked at the types of industry that I wanted to go into. I just put my name down for them really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and did you say it’s the design side that you want to go into more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do much research into the different companies then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah I researched them a bit when I put my name down and then when I went to interview obviously I read up on them and stuff – but I only really had – I got a job pretty quickly so I didn’t have many interviews, so I didn’t research that many.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what type of work you’ll be doing when you get there? Have they told you much about what to expect?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’ll be doing – I’ll probably end – I’ll have several projects on the go all the time. Part of them long term, some short term and erm, just general – well, like they’ll have certain problems like they want to save so much money on this, or they want to get this out but – and I’ll just – it’s up to me to do it, and research it and sort it out, kind of thing. I mean – obviously it’s not going to be huge and major but I mean like one project that I’m going to get which is – the girl that’s there at the moment, she’s going to – and they’ll try and – they have kind of 8 machines, for sort of – they all do the same thing, and they want to use 6 but increase the output, so that’s one big thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what are you most looking forward to about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Working with real people. Big people – because it is a bit of a bubble, and you don’t see many people, and that’ll be nice to like actually go out and just like learn stuff properly, rather than just be sat in a lecture theatre – actually really learn stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK and is there anything that you’re apprehensive or concerned about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no, I’ve heard well, as long as I’m confident in myself, then I’ll be alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how involved were the university in helping you find a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They were really good erm they kind of – obviously the companies approach the department and say we want to interview on this day. But there’s a board on – next to the notice board, with lists up, like name of company, where it is and you just write your name down on there. And then all your – the department sends all your CV’s – CV’s that are on the list, to the company who kind of choose some people they want to interview. So they’re brilliant like that because a lot of people actually have to go out and send out their own CV and do all that, but our department were brilliant, absolutely brilliant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there is anything else that they should be doing or shouldn’t be doing, to help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I mean they’ve got – they’ve also got all the research and things because all these companies obviously send out their things and you can look at all that. I don’t think so – I mean they’ve obviously been doing that kind of thing for years because they’ve got it down to a fine art now. So no, I don’t think they can do anymore.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, your department’s obviously one of the better ones. You mentioned about getting sponsorship. (yeah). Are you sponsored at the minute or is that…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, well the company that I’m going to, offered me sponsorship so – and that’s just while I’m doing my degree.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of having sponsorship?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The only advantage is money. There’s no disadvantages because I don’t have to work for them when I graduate. So it’s a really weird one. I can’t understand that but that’s fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: They must hope that you will work for them, or something?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean it – cos in the contract it just kind of says I’m not obliged to work there but if there’s an opening, then chances are I’ll get the job over someone else. So it’s a weird one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you get on OK on your placement would you be happy to go and work for them when you’ve finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Different location, but yeah. Because their company’s – they work well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, what do you see yourself doing then in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh God. Let’s have a think. I’ll probably have been working for 2 years.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you will be in the chemical engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I should think so. I should think so. I’ll know in a few months – if I don’t I might do a second degree, but I don’t know – yeah, if I’m working it’ll probably be that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about more long term, do you think that you’d like to go down the managerial route or become more specialist?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Become specialised. Well no – long term, I’d like to retire young. And then like, do something like coaching and stuff – that’d be fun. But, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what then would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ideal career? Oh, design engineer would be quite nice – an amazing hockey coach – I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in chemical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that in terms of getting into the industry and once you’re in the industry for moving upwards?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, cos I mean usually like – from what I’ve seen – and a company will have sort of 3 or 4 mechanical engineers and 1 chemical engineer. So if you’re like the chemical engineer then obviously you’re a lot – you know, there’s 4 of them, there’s only 1 of you, they’re not going to get rid of you unless – well, it’s pretty highly unlikely that they’re gonna get rid of you, when they have job cuts and things as well, so in that respect…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you have done anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d probably have done slightly different ‘A’ levels.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why? If you’d done different ‘A’ levels, do you still think you’d be where you are now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d be at [this university]. Sometimes I wonder why I did chemical engineering. Erm, I probably would have done like sports science and chemistry. I don’t know – it is a lot of work. I’m like, I’d like to not do as much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But it’s interesting to hear you say that. Because you think you probably will go into the chemical engineering industry, but there probably are other things that you could do.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Ideally I’d work for sort of 9 months in a proper job and for 3 months I’d – I’d love to do something outside but it’s just like you don’t really have to think about it – it’s easy – easy on the brain, that would be quite good, because I love being outside, doing adventure schemes, but only like a very few people can do that. And I know a couple of people that do, which is probably why I’m like, so envious of them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But do you think that’s not a realistic option to you then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. The chances are slim. If the opportunity came up then I’d do it. But I’m not – I wouldn’t – it wouldn’t bother me if I don’t ever do it, kind of thing, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the chemical engineering industry or your experience of it so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That’s a tough one. Erm, (long pause) it depends what you look at though. Like it depends which kind of bit of the industry you look at. Erm, diverse, (long pause).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. .

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is masculine just because of the numbers of males in the industry or do you think it’s more than that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Generally, the numbers of males in the industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it’ll stay like that or do you think that there will be more women coming into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think gradually, there will be more women in the industry but it’ll always be male dominated – always. Certainly for – well, while I’m alive I should think, to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because that’s the way it’s always been – very traditional people aren’t we?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. But it’s changed in other industries, like in medicine and law and things like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s just – I don’t know, I just think it always will be in our lives.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s about the type of work you are doing as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That it’s perceived as masculine work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, cos I mean you could – you could work on like – well, people work on an oil rig, and there’s chemical engineers on there and there’s no women on there (yeah) so – and then like if you look at the forces as well. You get a – if you get a couple of – well, any engineers in there, in the forces – well, it is male dominated anyway there, isn’t it? (yeah) And then petro-chemicals again – ‘cos I wouldn’t work in – cos a lot – well no one on my course really wants to go in petro-chemicals but a couple are, but that’s just because I suppose how you see it and how you think about things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that women that have done chemical engineering degrees, take it a different route to males then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d say women tend to go into pharmaceuticals and food more, and men kind of more petro-chemical that kind of thing, more blokey stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the fact that it is so masculine will cause you any problems or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why not? Do you think that’s because you’ve made a decision to sort of stick to the design side or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think whatever area I work in, if it was full of men, it wouldn’t bother me at all but that’s probably just because of my personality and just probably because I play sport as well. It’s just something about my character I suppose, I don’t know. But it just doesn’t bother me – it really doesn’t bother me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it might bother men that you’re working with though? That you’re a woman in their environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably. They can deal with it. Yeah, probably – maybe a little bit, gradually less and less I think. But yeah, probably – a tiny bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But that doesn’t bother you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that’s everything thank you very much.
